opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it has to be a shared, ever-growing library of reusable abstractions. That's really the key idea. Today, when you train a deep learning model, you're starting from scratch, or close to it, every time. You fit a big parametric curve to a dataset, and whatever the model learns is entangled in its weights. It's very hard to extract, reuse, or recombine. That's the opposite of what intelligence actually looks like.

If you look at how humans become intelligent, and how software engineering works, it's about accumulating modular building blocks. When a programmer faces a new problem, they don't rewrite everything from first principles. They pull in libraries and functions that other people have written and tested, and they recombine them in new ways. Over time, the useful new abstractions they develop get pushed back into that shared pool, and everyone benefits.

So I picture lifelong distributed learning as many agents, many instances of a system, each encountering new tasks and new situations in the world. Each one solves its problem by searching over combinations of existing abstractions, essentially doing program synthesis. When it finds something new that is general and reusable, that gets abstracted and added to a global library that all the other instances can draw on. The system as a whole keeps getting more capable, not because any single model gets bigger, but because the library of concepts keeps growing and getting better organized.

Architecturally, that means a hybrid. You'd have a discrete component: programs, symbolic structures, things you can compose and verify. And you'd have a deep learning component providing intuition: fast, approximate pattern recognition that guides the search through that huge combinatorial space, so you're not brute-forcing. Deep learning is very good at perception and fuzzy judgment, what we might call type one thinking. Discrete program search is good at the type two side: reasoning, planning, generalizing from very little data. You need both, tightly integrated.

And the "distributed" part matters a lot, because no single agent will encounter enough diversity in its lifetime to build up a truly broad library. Human civilization works the same way. Our individual brains aren't that impressive in isolation. What makes us powerful is that we're plugged into a cultural repository of abstractions built up over thousands of years. I think general AI will look more like that, a civilization-level process of accumulating and sharing knowledge, than like one giant monolithic model.

r001.rationale: The response describes many agents encountering different tasks, then abstracting new general, reusable solutions into shared building blocks for the library.

r002.rationale: It says newly abstracted abstractions are added to a global library that other instances can use, making the system more capable over time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that it's not going to look like what we have today. The current paradigm is: you collect a giant static dataset, you train one monolithic model offline, you freeze it, and you deploy it. That's fundamentally at odds with lifelong learning, where the system has to keep acquiring new knowledge and new skills continuously, from a stream of experience, without forgetting what it already knows, and ideally while getting more efficient at learning over time.

So architecturally, I think you need a few things. First, you need a separation between the part of the system that stores reusable abstractions and the part that does on-the-fly adaptation. Deep learning today conflates those. All knowledge is smeared across one set of weights, which is why you get catastrophic forgetting the moment you try to update it incrementally. What you want instead is something closer to a library, a repository of modular, composable building blocks, programs essentially, that the system can retrieve and recombine when it encounters a new situation. Learning a new task should mostly be a matter of search and composition over that library, with a small amount of new fitting, and the result of that search should be written back into the library so it's available next time.

Second, I think the adaptation process itself has to be more like program synthesis than like gradient descent. Gradient descent is a wonderful tool for interpolative problems, for fitting a continuous manifold, but it's a poor fit for acquiring discrete, symbolic, rule-like knowledge quickly from a handful of examples. Humans don't need ten thousand examples to learn a new rule. So I imagine a hybrid: deep learning modules providing perception and intuition, guiding a discrete search process that assembles new programs out of existing ones. The deep learning component makes the search tractable, the search component makes the learning data-efficient and compositional.

And third, when you say distributed, that's where it gets interesting. If you have many agents learning in many environments, they shouldn't each have to rediscover the same abstractions. The library I'm describing becomes a shared resource. Agents contribute new modules, and there's some process of consolidation, where redundant or overly specific modules get pruned and generalized. It starts to look less like a neural network and more like an evolving ecosystem of programs, or frankly like how human culture works. Most of what any individual knows wasn't learned from scratch, it was inherited. I think that's the right template. The architecture is a shared, growing library of abstractions, plus local learners that are good at retrieving, recombining, and extending it.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents learning across many environments, contributing modules to a shared library, and consolidating redundant or overly specific modules by pruning and generalizing them.

r002.rationale: It says the result of learning is written back into the library for future use, and describes the library as shared and growing, letting agents retrieve, recombine, and extend its modules.

astra-6.text:
I think you would need an architecture that is modular, where different parts of the system can learn relatively independently, and where you can recombine what they have learned. Because if every new thing you learn requires updating the entire system, you have a problem with interference. You also have a problem with coordination when learning is distributed across many different agents.

So the question becomes: what is the unit of knowledge that these agents exchange? You probably don’t want it to be just a set of weight updates. You want something that can be reused in a new context, something like a program or an abstraction, with some way of determining when it applies.

Then you need a mechanism for taking these pieces, adapting them, and composing them to solve new problems. You could imagine neural networks doing perception and guiding that process, coupled with a more explicit space of reusable abstractions. But I think the difficult part is learning the right abstractions and organizing them over time. Modularity alone doesn’t solve that.

r001.rationale: The response describes reusable programs or abstractions exchanged among agents, but does not say to create them by abstracting commonalities across distributed problem-solving experiences.

r002.rationale: The response discusses adapting and composing reusable pieces, but does not describe feeding newly abstracted building blocks back into the system to increase its capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it will require a fairly modular architecture. You want a system that can acquire new skills without having to modify everything it already knows, and that can reuse those skills in new situations. So you need some way of separating knowledge into pieces that can be recombined, rather than storing everything in one undifferentiated set of weights.

And if learning is distributed, there’s also the question of what gets communicated. You probably don’t want agents merely exchanging parameter updates. You want them to exchange knowledge in a form that another agent can interpret and use, even if it has a different history. Programs are an interesting candidate for that: they’re compact, compositional, and they can express abstractions.

So I would look toward a combination of learned representations and something more explicit and program-like, with mechanisms for deciding what to retain, what to share, and when a previously learned abstraction applies. But I don’t think we have a complete architecture for that yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modular, reusable knowledge and program-like abstractions, but does not describe abstracting commonalities across distributed problem-solving experiences to create building blocks.

r002.rationale: It mentions retaining and sharing knowledge, but does not state that newly abstracted building blocks are fed back into the system to increase its capabilities.
